auxiliary_material: The review provides extensive mechanistic context for how metabolites like SCFAs, Inosine, and TMAO modulate immune responses (e.g., HDAC inhibition, A2aR signaling, mTOR pathway regulation) which may influence the TME. It also notes controversies, such as the negative correlation of butyrate with CTLA-4 efficacy, emphasizing the complexity of metabolite-host interactions. These details help frame the biological plausibility of metabolite-TME interactions, even though direct tissue quantification is absent.
outline_action: Search for primary clinical studies performing targeted metabolomics (LC-MS/MS, Mass Spectrometry Imaging) on human tumor tissue biopsies from ICI-treated cohorts. Prioritize studies that report absolute concentration values (e.g., μM, ng/mg) of Inosine, Butyrate, or SCFAs in the TME and analyze correlations with ORR/PFS/OS. Verify if any studies include paired tumor-serum analysis to bridge systemic and local metabolite levels.
remaining_gap: The gap requires primary studies reporting absolute quantitative concentrations of microbial metabolites (Inosine, Butyrate, SCFAs) measured directly in human tumor tissue (TME) or paired tumor-serum samples from ICI-treated patients. This material only reports concentrations in feces and plasma/serum from external cohorts cited by the authors; it does not provide data on metabolite concentrations within the tumor microenvironment itself. Furthermore, as a review article, it does not present original primary data meeting the specific methodological criteria of targeted metabolomics on tumor tissue.
useful_material: The study is a narrative review summarizing the role of gut microbial metabolites in cancer immunotherapy. It reports clinical observations where fecal Short-Chain Fatty Acids (SCFAs) concentrations were measured in cohorts of patients receiving PD-1 inhibitors (Nivolumab/Pembrolizumab). Specifically, it cites a cohort of 52 solid tumor patients and an NSCLC cohort of 11 patients, noting that higher fecal SCFA levels (acetate, propionate, butyrate, valerate) were associated with longer progression-free survival and beneficial effects. It also references a study on metastatic melanoma patients treated with anti-CTLA-4, where serum butyrate and propionate were inversely correlated with PFS/OS. The review details mechanisms for SCFAs, Inosine, TMAO, and Tryptophan metabolites, highlighting their potential as predictive biomarkers.
